wave_readiness_notes.line: Suggested, with 5 design review warnings to accept: DynamoDB DDB-AP-56 (user_emails, query -1103477891760818995): Set returned_attributes to ["id"] (a ProjectionExpression on id) so the application can compare it with the given id; id is a plain attribute, not part of the b; DynamoDB DDB-AP-52 (badges, queries -1688818047978558009, 5216308275152432321, -6894768671255151131): Either return ["id", "enabled"] so the application checks the flag, or put the check in a condition_expression/ProjectionExpression; update the description to m; DynamoDB ActionsByTargetUser, ActionsByActingUser, ActionsByTargetPost (user_actions): Record the null share of target_user_id, acting_user_id and target_post_id; keep each GSI only where it serves a pattern that justifies it (DDB-AP-63, -18, -19); DynamoDB site_settings.id, DDB-AP-184, DDB-AP-182, SettingsById: Enforce id uniqueness with a sentinel item keyed by the id value. Write it in the same TransactWriteItems as the setting, with attribute_not_exists in its condi; DynamoDB post_custom_fields / DDB-AP-212: Add a sentinel item per (post_id, name) for the names the source's unique indexes cover, written in the same TransactWriteItems as the field with attribute_not_. If you do not accept them: revise the DynamoDB schema design in your modernization session and review it again.

effective_architecture.rule: Every engine and table claim in the summary must match effective_architecture: name a table under an engine only if that table is in the engine's tables list (the tables its assigned in-scope queries touch), never present an eliminated engine as part of the target, and do not generalise a table to an engine that merely shares a query group with it. A summary that attributes a table to an engine none of whose queries touch it is rejected and the deterministic summary is shown instead.

deterministic_summary:
Recommendation: move the discourse PostgreSQL database to four AWS services in three waves. Wave 1 moves it to Aurora PostgreSQL, which ends up serving 48.2% of the queries; wave 2 puts ElastiCache in front of 3 hot reads (25.1% of calls); wave 3 moves 42.0% of the queries to DynamoDB and 9.9% to DocumentDB. The projected cost of the full modernization is $536 per month at AWS Price List on-demand prices for us-east-1, retrieved 2026-11-04. No current cost was collected for the source database, so the plan claims no saving against it.

Risk: overall risk is high. The main exposure is a high-severity migration complexity risk on Aurora PostgreSQL: review it in the risk register before wave 1 starts.

Decision: approve wave 1. It is safe to approve: it moves the database 1:1 to Aurora PostgreSQL, the same engine family as PostgreSQL, with its current data model, and its cutover waits until schema and data parity is validated against the source. Approving wave 3 accepts its 5 design review warnings, listed in the roadmap.

assumptions: On-demand capacity mode for all target databases
Does not include data transfer, backups, or global tables
Reads the cache layer fronts are also billed on their owner engines, as if every one missed the cache (conservative)
39 source tables no in-scope query reads (<0.01 GB) are stored on Aurora PostgreSQL, where wave 1 moves them

The DynamoDB figure includes $0.51/mo for the design's 59 global secondary indexes at on-demand prices: $0.00 of storage (each index's item count times its projected item size plus 100 bytes of index overhead per item) and $0.51 of index writes (one for each put or delete whose item may set the index's keys, two for an update that changes an index key or does not say what it changes, one for an update that changes only a projected attribute, billed at the standard rate per 1 KB of the projected item, on average load with the collected rows per call, an average of exactly zero counted as one row). Index reads are not added, since each is one of its query's reads and already priced, and the free tier is left out
DynamoDB reads are priced eventually consistent, except transactions, which are priced at transactional rates.

risks.description: [dynamodb] trigger: category_settings_require_reply_approval_readonly needs application-side logic on DynamoDB.
risks.mitigation: Implement as application logic: The source trigger raises an error on INSERT or UPDATE of require_reply_approval. The application layer rejects writes to require_reply_approval and require_topic_approval, because DynamoDB has no triggers.

risks.description: [dynamodb] trigger: category_settings_require_topic_approval_readonly needs application-side logic on DynamoDB.
risks.mitigation: Implement as application logic: The source trigger raises an error on INSERT or UPDATE of require_topic_approval. The application layer rejects the write, or an IAM condition on dynamodb:Attributes denies it.

risks.description: [dynamodb] trigger: topic_timers_topic_id_readonly needs application-side logic on DynamoDB.
risks.mitigation: Implement as application logic: The trigger rejects changes to topic_id. The application stops writing topic_id on UpdateItem and adds the condition expression `attribute_not_exists(topic_id) OR topic_id = :topic_id` to any write that carries it.

risks.description: [aurora_postgresql] 1 query uses a leading-wildcard LIKE or a regular expression on Aurora PostgreSQL: SELECT "user_custom_fields".* FROM "user_custom_fields" INNER JOIN user_fields…. Aurora PostgreSQL indexes a leading-wildcard LIKE and a regular expression with a pg_trgm trigram index (GIN or GiST), an extension to create (the PostgreSQL documentation of pg_trgm describes its index support for LIKE, ILIKE, ~ and ~*).
risks.mitigation: Create the pg_trgm extension and a GIN trigram index on the column (CREATE EXTENSION pg_trgm), which serves this LIKE, word searches included; full-text search (to_tsvector) also ranks word matches.

risks.description: Wave 3: 528 queries read 133 tables on an engine that does not own them. 436 of them read a copy of 83 tables that CDC keeps current from Aurora PostgreSQL, DocumentDB and DynamoDB across 6 engine pairs, so a read there can miss a recent write. The other 50 tables are written by no captured query, so a one-time copy serves them.
risks.mitigation: Before Wave 3 starts, set up CDC for each engine pair the sources of truth section lists, and send any read that must see its own write to its source of truth; copy the read-only tables once and confirm nothing outside the captured workload writes them. Compare the row counts on both sides. See the Wave 3 gate in the roadmap.

risks.description: Wave 3: 398 queries were decided by less than 5 points, and 102 more were exact ties a routing rule settled: Aurora PostgreSQL keeps 98 close calls and 44 ties over DynamoDB; DocumentDB takes 125 close calls over Aurora PostgreSQL; Aurora PostgreSQL keeps 71 close calls and 32 ties over DocumentDB; DynamoDB takes 63 close calls and 14 ties over DocumentDB; DynamoDB takes 34 close calls over Aurora PostgreSQL; DocumentDB takes 7 close calls and 12 ties over DynamoDB. A small change in the scores moves them.
risks.mitigation: Confirm the engine for these queries in the assignment review before Wave 3 starts, using the close calls section; move any that fit the runner-up better.

risks.description: [aurora_postgresql] 1 source object carries over to Aurora PostgreSQL with the schema: 1 trigger. This rests on Aurora PostgreSQL being the source's engine family; the collector reports no feature compatibility, so the schema design's note for each says what application work it needs.
risks.mitigation: Test each one on Aurora PostgreSQL against the source's behaviour and do the application work the schema design's note for it names. See the Wave 1 gate in the roadmap.

risks.description: [aurora_postgresql] The Aurora PostgreSQL schema design records 1 trade-off to review, listed under Migration trade-offs in the engineering report.
risks.mitigation: Review this trade-off with the team that builds Aurora PostgreSQL before Wave 1 starts, and test each one the application depends on.
details: Source is PostgreSQL, so every table, column type, primary key, index and foreign key carries over as it is. Three indexes are added on foreign key columns that hot queries filter on: categories.parent_category_id, category_groups.category_id and chat_messages.user_id

risks.description: [documentdb] The DocumentDB schema design records 13 trade-offs to review, listed under Migration trade-offs in the engineering report.
risks.mitigation: Review these trade-offs with the team that builds DocumentDB before Wave 3 starts, and test each one the application depends on.
details: Columns that point at users, posts, topics, categories and groups become plain id fields, because those parent tables are served by other engines
Every source table becomes its own collection, and the notes table is embedded in the reviewables collection as an array named notes, capped at 50 entries

Filters that use not-equal, not-in or a negated pattern cannot use an index for that condition: the translation override status test, the token log action exclusion, and the not-null test on rejected emails
Indexes are listed for the observed queries and the primary key only. Source unique constraints that no access pattern names (for example on sitemaps.name and uploads.sha1) are not in the list

Row counts for most tables are not in the source statistics, so the figures use the stated assumption of size over declared row width. The api_keys average of 71.68 KB comes from its address array column
Source timestamps become ISODate values, network address columns become strings, JSON columns become sub-documents, array columns become native arrays, and the sprite bytes column becomes binary data
The API key lookup is the busiest statement at 3.27 requests per second and reads the whole document, so its index is on the hash and _id and does not cover the read
The color scheme insert no longer gets a database-generated id
The sidebar sections order uses a computed expression, so the pipeline computes a flag and sorts on it after the index matches the public sections

The source extension functions (text matching, key-value, vector and case-insensitive text helpers) and the three trigger functions belong to tables that other engines serve, so none move with this design
The themes collection has an index on color_scheme_id, which routing assumed for the color scheme lookup
Three joins are served with one equality lookup stage each: form templates through category links, themes through child links, and user API keys through their client
Two source statements test a column against null where the column cannot be null, and one tests the primary key against null. They return no rows

The tag name, tag slug and tag group name are copied into category_tags and category_tag_groups, replacing the two joins of queries `-3427295` and `5631712`
The target-not-equal read (query `3757647435148076712`) is a Query on the identifier partition with a FilterExpression on target

The token lookup by hash (query `54780307`) becomes a GetItem, with confirmed, expired, scope and created_at checked in the application

The tsvector column search_data of topic_search_data and user_search_data is not stored; the items hold raw_data, locale and version
The two COUNT queries on user_actions (queries `-8883206` and `-2719095`) run as Query calls with Select=COUNT on ActionsByType (action_type, created_at)

The upsert in query `6668674146221133871` (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET count = count + excluded.count) becomes UpdateItem with ADD count on the date and req_type key
The users table is a placeholder owned by another design group, keyed by user_id, with the UsersByUsernameLower index on username_lower for query `8270933069653201035`
The users table keeps the source id as its partition key (user_id) and serves username lookups through the UsersByUsernameLower and UsersByUsername GSIs
The value and value_baked text columns stay inline in the item; the table's avg_row_size_bytes is 3383 against the 400 KB item limit

The visibility check (query `83441274`) is split across tables: a GetItem on categories, a Query on category_groups by category_id, and a lookup of the user's groups in group_users, which design group 9 owns; no placeholder for group_users is defined here
The visit count on user_visits is a Query with Select=COUNT on user_id and a visited_at range, with posts_read as a filter, with no counter item
ThemeFieldById projects KEYS_ONLY because it only finds the table key for the update by id
Three GSIs on users: UsersByUsernameLower and UsersByUsername project ALL; UsersByUploadedAvatar is sparse and projects keys only
Timestamps are stored as ISO 8601 strings, the JSON payload as a map, and the sequence ids as application-generated numbers
TopicUsersByUser (partition user_id, sort topic_id, INCLUDE notifications_reason_id and total_msecs_viewed) serves the two key-scoped writes on topic_users by user_id
Update by id (query `18968104`) uses the SettingsById index, which holds the keys only
UploadsByUrl indexes url with upload_id as sort key and projects all attributes, serving query `-8400597078852665671`

`ai_agents` keeps the source id as the partition key because query `-9107418073878310695` reads by id; `system_prompt` and `description` stay inline in the item, whose measured average is 3755 bytes against the 400 KB item limit

`sitemaps` and `application_requests` and `web_crawler_requests` are keyed on their natural unique keys (sitemaps.name; date with req_type; date with user_agent), which are unique, NOT NULL and stable, instead of the generated id

risks.description: [elasticache] The ElastiCache schema design records 6 trade-offs to review, listed under Migration trade-offs in the engineering report.
risks.mitigation: Review these trade-offs with the team that builds ElastiCache before Wave 2 starts, and test each one the application depends on.
details: A cached user row stays until the owner write path deletes its key, and for at most the 300 second TTL if that delete fails
API key rows use a 60 second TTL, shorter than the other keys, because they gate authentication
An API key with no scopes is cached as an empty JSON array for 300 seconds
Every key is read with a single-key command, so no key carries a hash tag
The cached API key row holds last_used_at, which the owner updates on every use of a key
User rows are cached as one serialized string per lowercase username instead of a hash with one field per column

risks.description: [documentdb] Routing assumes a redesign for 1 query on DocumentDB: it scored it with 1 key the source does not have, so the plan holds only if the DocumentDB design adds it. 1 key has no cardinality statistics.
risks.mitigation: Give each of this query the keys routing assumed in the DocumentDB design, check a key with few or unknown distinct values for hot partitions, and serve none of them as a scan. See the Wave 3 gate in the roadmap.
details: A key on themes.color_scheme_id: read as key-scoped 1:N read instead of ad hoc filter.

risks.description: [dynamodb] Routing assumes a redesign for 9 queries on DynamoDB: it scored them with 7 keys the source does not have, so the plan holds only if the DynamoDB design adds them. The redesign also removes the frequent-full-scan and wide-transaction findings the source shows. 7 keys have no cardinality statistics.
risks.mitigation: Give each of these queries the keys routing assumed in the DynamoDB design, check a key with few or unknown distinct values for hot partitions, and serve none of them as a scan. See the Wave 3 gate in the roadmap.
details: A key on reviewable_claimed_topics.user_id: read as key-scoped 1:N read instead of ad hoc filter. With a key on reviewable_claimed_topics.user_id the write is key scoped (changes the rows one user_id value of reviewable_claimed_topics addresses, a key that is not unique: a key-scoped multi-item write (a Query plus a batch write)): one Query on that key and a batch write.
A whole read of a small reference table, which the design keeps as one item collection or caches.

Keys on category_custom_fields.name, directory_columns.name, email_tokens.email, push_subscriptions.user_id, theme_settings.theme_id and topic_embeds.topic_id: each read as key-scoped 1:N read instead of ad hoc filter.

risks.description: [dynamodb] DynamoDB serves 13 statements on 10 tables poorly (scores 11 to 26, below 50): retention delete (6), consistency repair sweep (3), orphan clean-up (2), delete by any of several references (1) and duplicate clean-up (1). A table has one writer, so each moves with the other statements that write its table.
risks.mitigation: Design these statements in DynamoDB for what they are for, the target's own way, not as a copy of the source's set-based SQL; each statement's detail names the approach. See the Wave 3 gate in the roadmap.

risks.description: [aurora_postgresql] We could not translate 269 routines automatically; migrate them yourself before wave 1. They are 260 functions, 6 procedures, 3 triggers. This is a to-do and holds no wave. Why: no exact code was collected (266); a check failed (3); names a table the collection does not have (3).
risks.mitigation: Migrate these routines yourself before wave 1, then check them again. See the Wave 1 gate in the roadmap.

mitigation_strategies: Load-test the queries behind RISK-004 on Aurora PostgreSQL with production-scale data. The cutover is your responsibility.
Apply the mitigations of RISK-001, RISK-002 and RISK-003.

After wave 1 (Aurora PostgreSQL): compare the latency of 1654 queries with their source baseline (weighted average 0.06 ms) and check the engine sustains the collected traffic of 39.1 requests/s before starting wave 2.
After wave 2 (ElastiCache): track the cache hit rate for the 3 hot reads it fronts on Aurora PostgreSQL (25.1% of calls, 9.8 calls/s) and compare their latency with the source before starting wave 3.

After wave 3 (DynamoDB and DocumentDB): compare the latency of 857 queries with their source baseline (weighted average 0.04 ms) and check the engine sustains the collected traffic of 25.1 requests/s.

resolved_risks.description: [documentdb] Queries joining 3 or more tables. Each join becomes a $lookup stage that reads the joined collection for the documents flowing through it, one stage per collection, with a nested-loop, hash or sort-merge algorithm (Amazon DocumentDB Developer Guide, Functional differences, $lookup); correlated $lookup needs DocumentDB 8.0.2 or later.
resolved_risks.reason: the queries run as SQL on Aurora PostgreSQL

resolved_risks.description: [documentdb] Queries with NOT IN, <>, !=, NOT EXISTS, which map to $ne/$nin/$nor. Query planner version 2 and later use indexes for $ne, $nin and $not, so a negation is no worse on DocumentDB than on an engine where it is rarely index-selective (Amazon DocumentDB Developer Guide, Query planner).
resolved_risks.reason: the queries run as SQL on Aurora PostgreSQL

resolved_risks.description: [documentdb] SQL window functions $setWindowFields serves (ROW_NUMBER, RANK, running totals): DocumentDB 8.0.2 or later on an instance-based cluster. LAG and LEAD ($shift) and NTILE (no bucketing window operator) run on no version, so they are a hard capability gap, not this entry (Amazon DocumentDB Developer Guide, Supported MongoDB APIs, operations, and data types).
resolved_risks.reason: the queries run as SQL on Aurora PostgreSQL

resolved_risks.description: [documentdb] Queries with correlated subqueries. A correlated $lookup (let/pipeline) runs its sub-pipeline for each input document, and needs DocumentDB 8.0.2 or later on an instance-based cluster (Amazon DocumentDB Developer Guide, Supported MongoDB APIs, operations, and data types); otherwise pre-denormalize.
resolved_risks.reason: the queries run as SQL on Aurora PostgreSQL

resolved_risks.description: [documentdb] Moved to DynamoDB: Queries with correlated subqueries. A correlated $lookup (let/pipeline) runs its sub-pipeline for each input document, and needs DocumentDB 8.0.2 or later on an instance-based cluster (Amazon DocumentDB Developer Guide, Supported MongoDB APIs, operations, and data types); otherwise pre-denormalize.
resolved_risks.reason: the queries moved to DynamoDB, whose schema design serves all of them

resolved_risks.description: [documentdb] Self-referential FKs or recursive queries. $graphLookup runs on DocumentDB 8.0 instance-based clusters, not on 5.0 or earlier and not on elastic clusters (Amazon DocumentDB Developer Guide, Supported MongoDB APIs, operations, and data types).
resolved_risks.reason: the queries run as SQL on Aurora PostgreSQL

resolved_risks.description: [dynamodb] The first rows of a whole table in some order (ORDER BY with a row limit and no key value). A DynamoDB Scan returns items in no particular order, so the first rows by any order need every item read and sorted by the application (Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide, Scanning tables).
resolved_risks.reason: the queries run as SQL on Aurora PostgreSQL

resolved_risks.description: [dynamodb] Moved to DocumentDB: The first rows of a whole table in some order (ORDER BY with a row limit and no key value). A DynamoDB Scan returns items in no particular order, so the first rows by any order need every item read and sorted by the application (Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide, Scanning tables).

resolved_risks.description: [dynamodb] GROUP BY, HAVING, or an aggregate over rows no key anchors or over a join (one key's COUNT or SUM is a Query on that key, not this pattern). DynamoDB has no server-side aggregation: a Query or Scan can only count the items it reads (Select = COUNT), so a grouped result needs the application layer, pre-computed aggregates or a separate analytics store (Amazon DynamoDB API Reference, Query).
resolved_risks.reason: the queries run as SQL on Aurora PostgreSQL

resolved_risks.description: [dynamodb] A write wider than one transaction: more than 100 items, or rows a range, join, subquery or a filter with no key anchor picks (a write by a non-unique key column is a key-scoped Query plus batch write, not this). DynamoDB TransactWriteItems holds up to 100 items and 4 MB across tables (Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide, Amazon DynamoDB Transactions).
resolved_risks.reason: the schema design covers every flagged query
